After Shi Hu had invaded and withdrawn, he still intended to annex territory and sent his general Deng Heng with tens of thousands of men to camp at Le'an, making ready to attack and take new territory.
The verbs after 既還 continue 石季龍: he still meant to annex land and sent Deng Heng. Murong Huang is not in the sentence; s0008 has Chui facing Heng, which fits a Later Zhao general, not a Yan one.

Muyu Gen urged Jun, "What the prince says comes once in an age and must not be missed."
The speaker is 慕輿根. 慕輿 is the surname Muyu, not the Murong (慕容) clan name.

有聲于梁、楚之南 names Liang and Chu. The Huai is not in the Chinese.

Made Colonel-Director of Retainers a second time, every man of rank in the Yan court thronged his gates.
再為司隸 is the capital-province inspectorate, conventionally Colonel-Director of Retainers (司隸校尉), not a vague 'Director of the Capital'.

Fu Jian refused; he appointed Chui General of the Champions and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Bindu with five hundred households at Huayin.
賓都侯 is Marquis of Bindu: 都 is du, so Bintu misreads the fief name.

Muyu Gen said to Jun, "The prince's words are a once-in-a-thousand-years moment and must not be lost."
慕輿根 has the surname Muyu (慕輿), not Murong.

Again made Colonel-Director of Retainers, none among the false princes and dukes downward failed to crowd his gate.
司隸 here is the Colonel-Director of Retainers, not 'Director of the Capital'.

Jian did not follow this; he made Chui General of the Champions and enfeoffed him as Marquis of Bindu with a fief of five hundred households at Huayin.
賓都 is Bindu; Bintu is a wrong reading of 都.

Fu Jian refused; he sent Li Man, Min Liang, and Yin Guo with three thousand men to escort Chui, posted Shi Yue at Ye and Zhang Hao at Bingzhou.

Nong won Kuruguan Wei in Shangdang to the west and Qitegui at Dong'e to the east; each brought tens of thousands until their host passed a hundred thousand.

The Marquis of Changle is the emperor's heir, his virtue beyond Tang and Wei, the pillar east of the mountains—he will not meekly yield you a hundred cities!
The Duke of Changle is the emperor's eldest son, his virtue beyond Tang and Wei, the pillar east of the mountains—he will not meekly yield you a hundred cities!
長樂公 is Duke of Changle; 主上之元子 is the sovereign's eldest son, not a generic 'heir'.

The Princess of Changle is the sovereign's eldest son, his virtue surpassing Tang and Wei, holding the duty east of Shan—he is the court's bulwark; how can he meekly hand the general a hundred cities!
The Duke of Changle is the sovereign's eldest son, his virtue surpassing Tang and Wei, holding the duty east of Shan—he is the court's bulwark; how can he meekly hand the general a hundred cities!
The cut is 長樂公 / 主上之元子. Reading 公主 invents a princess who is not in the sentence.
Bin again sent the Chief Clerk of Henan Guo Tong to persuade Chui, and Chui then agreed.
Bin again sent his Chief Clerk Guo Tong of Henan to persuade Chui, and Chui then agreed.
長史河南郭通 is Bin's chief clerk, Guo Tong of Henan. 河南 is origin, not a 'Chief Clerk of Henan' office.
Fu Pi sent the attendant Jiang Rang to say, "When the emperor lost his throne you guarded him; your loyalty outshone the ancients.
Fu Pi sent the attendant Jiang Rang to say, "When the imperial carriage was routed you guarded the emperor; your loyalty outshone the ancients.
大駕失據 is the imperial cortege losing its footing (the Huainan rout), not the emperor losing the throne; 保衛鑾輿 is guarding the carriage.

He styled his headquarters the Commandery Office with four aides; nobles and officials addressed him as lord; enfeoffments followed royal precedent; Zhai Bin became Grand General Who Establishes Righteousness and Prince of Henan;

He styled his headquarters the Commandery Office with four aides; nobles and officials styled themselves his subjects; enfeoffments followed royal precedent; Zhai Bin became Grand General Who Establishes Righteousness and Prince of Henan;
王公已下稱臣 means princes and dukes downward styled themselves his subjects, not that they addressed him as lord.

He ordered that the unified headquarters be called the Commandery Office, with four assistants; princes and dukes downward called him lord; all enfeoffments and appointments were as for a king; Zhai Bin was made Grand General Who Establishes Righteousness and Prince of Henan;

He ordered that the unified headquarters be called the Commandery Office, with four assistants; princes and dukes downward styled themselves his subjects; all enfeoffments and appointments were as for a king; Zhai Bin was made Grand General Who Establishes Righteousness and Prince of Henan;
稱臣 is to declare themselves subjects (臣), not to call him lord.
Last summer Huan Chong died; our plans cleared like clouds; at Xiangcheng we took tens of thousands of heads—this was your divine strategy and my small share of dying for you.
Last summer Huan Chong came on to his ruin; our plans cleared like clouds; at Yuncheng we took tens of thousands of heads—this was your divine strategy and my small share of dying for you.
桓沖送死 is a doomed offensive, not a report that Chong died; 鄖城 is Yuncheng, not Xiangcheng.

Last summer Huan Chong came to his death; in one plan it was like clouds dispersed; returning to attack Xiangcheng, captives and severed ears numbered in the tens of thousands—this is truly Your Majesty's divine calculation, and also your foolish servant's effect of forgetting death.

Last summer Huan Chong came to his death; in one plan it was like clouds dispersed; returning to attack Yuncheng, captives and severed ears numbered in the tens of thousands—this is truly Your Majesty's divine calculation, and also your foolish servant's effect of forgetting death.
鄖城 is Yuncheng (鄖 yun). Xiangcheng would be 襄城.
I was ordered north and bound by the Marquis of Changle.
I was ordered north and bound by the Duke of Changle.
受制長樂 points to Fu Pi as 長樂公, a duke, not a marquis.
Your servant received the edict to tour the north and was constrained by the Marquis of Changle.
Your servant received the edict to tour the north and was constrained by the Duke of Changle.
長樂 is the Duke of Changle; 公, not 侯.
I asked the Marquis of Changle to send all his men to the emperor and release them with honor; Pi clung to his obstinacy and would not bend.
I asked the Duke of Changle to send all his men to the emperor and release them with honor; Pi clung to his obstinacy and would not bend.
長樂公 is the Duke of Changle.

I wished to have the Marquis of Changle send all his host to the rescue and dismiss them with ceremony, but Pi obstinately held the will of a common man and did not comprehend the principle of change.
I wished to have the Duke of Changle send all his host to the rescue and dismiss them with ceremony, but Pi obstinately held the will of a common man and did not comprehend the principle of change.
長樂公 is the Duke of Changle, not a marquis.
At Luoyang the Plain Duke Fu Hui would not trust me.
At Luoyang, Fu Hui, Duke of Pingyuan, would not trust me.
平原公 is the fief-title Duke of Pingyuan, not 'Plain Duke'. The proposed string needs commas around the title.
When I reached Luoyang, the Plain Duke Hui again would not trust or accept me.
When I reached Luoyang, Hui, Duke of Pingyuan, again would not trust or accept me.
平原公 is Duke of Pingyuan, not 'Plain Duke'. A comma is needed after the title.
Only for Changle and the Plain Duke, still young when they met you in the Two Capitals—we regret their counsel was not to our mind; that is all."
Only for Changle and the Duke of Pingyuan, still young when they met you in the Two Capitals—we regret their counsel was not to our mind; that is all."
平原 is Fu Hui as Duke of Pingyuan; 'Plain Duke' translates the fief as an adjective.

Only the Marquis of Changle and the Plain Duke, in years not yet established, met you in the Two Capitals—we regret that their planning and conduct did not match Our heart; this is the only thing regretted."

Only the Duke of Changle and the Duke of Pingyuan, in years not yet established, met you in the Two Capitals—we regret that their planning and conduct did not match Our heart; this is the only thing regretted."
長樂 and 平原 are the Dukes of Changle and Pingyuan (Fu Pi and Fu Hui), not a marquis and a 'Plain Duke'.
I would have made you chief minister and marquis of a commandery to repay your merit—why has Bo Yi shattered his honor and Liu Hui turned debauched!
I would have made you chief minister and marquis of a commandery to repay your merit—why has Bo Yi shattered his honor and Liu Xiahui turned debauched!
柳惠 is the stock pairing of Liu Xiahui (柳下惠) with Bo Yi, not an otherwise unknown Liu Hui.

We were about to entrust you with the office of chief minister and enfeoff you as marquis of a commandery, hoping broadly to cross hardship and respectfully repay your merit—why has Bo Yi suddenly destroyed his icy integrity and willow Hui instantly become a debauched man!

We were about to entrust you with the office of chief minister and enfeoff you as marquis of a commandery, hoping broadly to cross hardship and respectfully repay your merit—why has Bo Yi suddenly destroyed his icy integrity and Liu Xiahui instantly become a debauched man!
柳惠 is Liu Xiahui. 'willow Hui' reads 柳 as the tree instead of the name.
At seventy you turn bandit, live a traitor, die a rebel, poison the living and dead—the pain of the central plains, what pain like it!
Now, nearing old age, you turn bandit, live a traitor, die a rebel, poison the living and dead—the pain of the central plains, what pain like it!
念卿垂老 is 'thinking of you as you near old age'. This sentence does not give the age seventy (that figure is in s0142).
The General Who Establishes the Commandery Xu Yan rebelled at Wuyi, drove and plundered more than four thousand men, and fled north to Youzhou.
The General Who Holds the Tally Xu Yan rebelled at Wuyi, drove and plundered more than four thousand men, and fled north to Youzhou.
建節將軍 is the General Who Establishes/Holds the Tally (節). 節 is not a commandery.

He appointed his left chief clerk Guan Wei of Ku Ruo, right chief clerk Duan Chong, dragon-cavalry commander Zhang Chong, and the governor of Zhongshan Feng Heng as Minister of the Civil Office; Murong De as Attendant-in-Ordinary, commander of all armies inside and outside the realm, and colonel of the masters of writing; the Pacifying General Murong Lin as Grand General of the Guards; and the remainder received posts according to merit.

He appointed his left chief clerk Kuruguan Wei, right chief clerk Duan Chong, dragon-cavalry commander Zhang Chong, and the governor of Zhongshan Feng Heng as Minister of Personnel; Murong De as Attendant-in-Ordinary, commander of all armies inside and outside the realm, and Colonel-Director of Retainers; the Pacifying General Murong Lin as Grand General of the Guards; and the remainder received posts according to merit.
庫辱官偉 is one name (Kuruguan Wei); 吏部尚書 is Minister of Personnel; 領司隸校尉 is concurrently Colonel-Director of Retainers, not a writing-office colonel.

Taking his Left Chief Clerk Guan Wei of Ku Ruo, Right Chief Clerk Duan Chong, and Dragon-Charger Zhang Chong, together with the Administrator of Zhongshan Feng Heng, as Minister of the Imperial Secretariat; Murong De as Attendant-in-Ordinary, Grand Commander of All Armies Within and Without, and Colonel Director of Convicts; the Pacifying General Murong Lin as Guards Grand General; the rest received appointments according to rank.

Taking his Left Chief Clerk Kuruguan Wei, Right Chief Clerk Duan Chong, and Dragon-Charger Zhang Chong, together with the Administrator of Zhongshan Feng Heng, as Minister of Personnel; Murong De as Attendant-in-Ordinary, Grand Commander of All Armies Within and Without, and Colonel-Director of Retainers; the Pacifying General Murong Lin as Guards Grand General; the rest received appointments according to rank.
The same three errors: Kuruguan Wei; 吏部尚書 as Minister of Personnel; 司隸校尉 as Colonel-Director of Retainers, not 'Director of Convicts'.

The erudites Liu Xiang and Dong Mi argued that the mother of Yao ranked only third among consorts and that the honored tomb was not that of Jiang Yuan, showing that the way of sage-kings put supreme impartiality above birth and rank.

The erudites Liu Xiang and Dong Mi argued that the mother of Yao ranked only third among consorts and that rank was not allowed to override Jiang Yuan, showing that the way of sage-kings put supreme impartiality above birth and rank.
不以貴陵薑嫄 uses 陵 'to override/press upon', not a tomb. Rank was not allowed to override Jiang Yuan.

The Erudites Liu Xiang and Dong Mi argued that Yao's mother held the third rank among consorts, that the honored tomb was not Jiang Yuan's, making clear that the way of sage-kings put supreme impartiality first.

The Erudites Liu Xiang and Dong Mi argued that Yao's mother held the third rank among consorts, that rank was not used to override Jiang Yuan, making clear that the way of sage-kings put supreme impartiality first.
陵 here is the verb 'override', not 'tomb'.
Chui smiled and said, "What can this boy do? I will be your butcher and kill him."
Chui smiled and said, "What can this boy do? I will kill him for you now."
The chapter graph 鯽 is a corrupt look-alike of 卿. CText reads 吾今为卿等杀之: 'I will now kill him for you gentlemen.' 'Butcher' is not in the Chinese.
Chui smiled and said, "How can this boy accomplish anything—I will be your carp and kill him for you."
Chui smiled and said, "How can this boy accomplish anything—I will now kill him for you gentlemen."
CText has 卿等, not 鯽. The line is 'I will now kill him for you gentlemen,' not a carp metaphor.
Yong thought it a feint and pulled all his men back to guard Zhatai Pass.
Yong thought it a feint and pulled all his men back to block the Zhi Pass in the Taihang.
杜太行軹關 is blocking the Taihang at Zhi Pass (軹關). Zhatai Pass is a ghost place-name.
Yong thought Chui was using a deceptive route to attack him and therefore gathered all his armies back to guard the Zhatai Pass at Huatai.
Yong thought Chui was using a deceptive route to attack him and therefore gathered all his armies back to block the Zhi Pass in the Taihang.
杜太行軹關 is the Zhi Pass in the Taihang. Neither Zhatai nor Huatai is written here.
Chui entered by Tianjing Pass and reached Hubei.
Chui entered by Tianjing Pass and reached Hubi.
壺壁 is Hubi (壁 bi), the same place as 壺避 in s0258. Hubei misreads 壁.
Chui advanced the army entering from Tianjing Pass, reaching Hubei.
Chui advanced the army entering from Tianjing Pass, reaching Hubi.
壺壁 is Hubi, not Hubei.
Nong swept Henan, took Lianqiu and Yangcheng, and the commanderies of Taishan and Langye fell away; he reached the sea, set magistrates, and returned.
Nong swept Henan, took Linqiu and Yangcheng, and the commanderies of Taishan and Langye fell away; he reached the sea, set magistrates, and returned.
廩丘 is Linqiu (廩 lǐn). Lianqiu is a wrong reading.

He sent Murong Nong to seize lands in Henan, attack Lianqiu and Yangcheng—all were taken; Taishan, Langye, and the various commanderies all abandoned their cities and fled in collapse; Nong advanced the army to the sea, set guards and magistrates, and returned.

He sent Murong Nong to seize lands in Henan, attack Linqiu and Yangcheng—all were taken; Taishan, Langye, and the various commanderies all abandoned their cities and fled in collapse; Nong advanced the army to the sea, set guards and magistrates, and returned.
廩丘 is Linqiu, not Lianqiu.
Murong De said, "The Wei, bloated by Canhe, despise the heir—strike now while your father's power is whole."
Murong De said, "The Wei, bloated by Canhe, despise the heir—strike now, while Your Majesty's sacred strategy is fresh, and crush their spirit."
慕容德 speaks to Chui: 宜及聖略，摧其銳志 is 'while the sacred strategy is still fresh, crush their keen will,' not 'while your father's power is whole.'

He sent Bao and Nong out by Tianmen, the northern expedition Murong Long and the western expedition Murong Sheng crossing Qing Mountain to strike the Wei Chenliu Duke Ni at Pingcheng, took it, and gathered his host of more than thirty thousand and returned.

He sent Bao and Nong out by Tianmen, the General Who Conquers the North Murong Long and the General Who Conquers the West Murong Sheng crossing Qing Mountain to strike the Wei Duke of Chenliu, Ni at Pingcheng, took it, and gathered his host of more than thirty thousand and returned.
征北 and 征西 are the generals' titles; 陳留公泥 is Ni, Duke of Chenliu, not a fused 'Chenliu Duke Ni' without the title structure.

unresolvedReferences.description: All Western dates in this chunk are event-contextual and come from external chronology (Yuwen 344, Shi Hu's invasion 338 and death 349, Jun's accession 348, Youzhou 350, imperial style 352, Wei's reign 360–370, Ke's death 367, Fangtou and Chui's flight 369, Luoyang and the fall of Ye 370, Huainan 383); the chapter itself gives no year wording in s0001–s0075.
The packet English makes Murong Huang the subject who sent Deng Heng; the Chinese subject is Shi Hu. Deng Heng is treated as Shi Hu's general and a repair is proposed.
郤𡙇 is identified as the Jin minister Xi Que (郤缺) by external identification; his dates are external.
The heir 全 is called Murong Ling 慕容令 in other histories (external); the chapter's form 全 is kept as the name.
太傅 (the Grand Tutor) who would not keep Chui is identified as Murong Ping by external knowledge of his office in 369; strongly inferred.
Ke's statement that the late emperor ranked him above Chui by birth order is taken as implying they were brothers (strongly inferred); 先帝 is linked to Murong Jun.
Tang and Shaokang are given qualitative traditional attestations; King Wu of Zhou receives broad external bounds (c. 1100–1000 BC) marked uncertain.
The Chang'an dice episode is bounded only as between the family's arrival in Qin (369/370) and 383 (external, derived).

The chapter dates Chui's proclamation to 太元八年 (the text's 乙太 is a conversion error for 以太). AD 383 is an external conversion; other histories put the proclamation in Taiyuan 9 (AD 384). Events before it (s0076–s0117) are dated AD 383 by derivation (after Huainan, before the proclamation) and later events as on or after AD 383.
歪 in s0083 and s0094 is a textual corruption of 丕 (Fu Pi); linked to Fu Pi.
The Marquis of Xinxing is identified as the deposed Yan ruler Murong Wei by external knowledge; the chapter itself calls him only the legitimate line and Chui's lord.
Kai and Shao are Chui's 'brother's sons'; which brother is not stated, so no intermediary person is created. Zhou is called 北子, an unexplained qualifier.
唐、衛 are taken as the Zhou royal brothers Shu Yu of Tang and Kang Shu of Wei (external identification, uncertain) with broad external bounds.
韓、白 give only surnames; identified as Han Xin and Bai Qi per the translation; their dates (196 BC, 260 BC) are external.
Jiang Rang calls Chui 'seventy'; recorded only as Rang's statement, not as a verified age.

The memorial, Fu Jian's reply and the rest of this chunk give no year wording; they are bounded as on or after AD 383 from the chapter's 太元八年 (external conversion). Specific external years are marked as external: Huan Chong's attack (summer 383), Murong Wei's killing (384), Liu Laozhi's relief of Ye (385), Koguryo's taking of Liaodong (385).
平原公 is Fu Hui's title, Duke of Pingyuan; 長樂 is Fu Pi, Duke of Changle. The packet English 'Plain Duke' and 'Marquis of Changle' are repaired.
淮陰 is identified as Han Xin (Marquis of Huaiyin), per the translation; ancient allusion dates (Han Xin 196 BC, Li Guang 119 BC, Gaixia 202 BC, Liu Xiahui 634 BC, King Wu bounds) are external.
柳惠 is taken as Liu Xiahui (external identification by standard pairing with Bo Yi). Bo Yi and Huandou receive qualitative legendary attestations.
Fu Pi's sonship to Fu Jian is only implied here (天性之念); recorded as strongly inferred.
垂老 in s0180 means 'nearing old age' (a pun on Chui's name) and is not linked as a name surface.

The chapter dates Chui's enthronement to 太元十一年 (乙太 is a conversion error for 以太); AD 386 is an external conversion. Units s0215–s0217 precede it and follow the 太元八年 entry, so they are bounded AD 383–386 (derived); s0218–s0247 follow it and are bounded on or after AD 386 (derived). External years are marked as external: Fu Pi's abandonment of Ye (385) and the Huatai campaign (392).
太原王 (whose son is Kai) is the former Prince of Taiyuan; the identification as Murong Ke (died 367) is external.

Lady Lan, Empress Duan (Huang's consort) and Murong Huang are dated only as before AD 386 (derived); the posthumous honors are recorded as posthumous-commemoration events. Murong Huang's death in 348 is external.
The Lady Duan made empress in s0226 is Chui's consort, distinct from Murong Huang's Empress Duan in s0296.
堅子 in s0240 means 'this boy' (豎子), not Fu Jian; 鯽 appears to be a corruption of 卿.
Murong Wei is dated before AD 386 (derived); his death in 384 is external.

Chui's death is dated 太元二十一年 in the chapter (乙太 is a conversion error for 以太); AD 396 is an external conversion. His birth year AD 326 is derived from 'aged seventy-one' by sui reckoning. Events s0248–s0286 are bounded AD 386–396 (derived); specific external years are marked as external: the Changzi campaign (394) and Canhe (395). The Pingcheng campaign is placed in 396 as part of the death-year narrative (external conversion).
The Wei Duke of Chenliu is named only as 泥 (Ni); no external identification is asserted.
壺避 in s0258 is a variant writing of 壺壁 (Hubi) in s0256.
Chengwu (posthumous title) and Shizu (temple name) are recorded as name surfaces of Murong Chui; the Jinshu labels the title 偽 (illegitimate).
